newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil cellular selloff seen on course.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil cellular selloff seen on course.

text.p: With one B Band concession sold and nine to go, Brazil on Wednesday was on course for a successful privatization of its promising cellular telephone sector, analysts said.
"Everything's on track," said Jacopo Valentino of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Brazil.
Investment bank analysts said the Communications Ministry's granting of a concession contract for B Band area 7 and release of names of qualified bidders for other areas were both positive steps.

A Canadian-led group's offer of 25.4 percent above the base price for area 7 covering rural central and western Brazil was positive but did not provide a benchmark for gauging bids on the remaining areas, they said.

Lone bidder Americel - made up of Bell Canada, a unit of BCE Inc ; Telesystem, also of Canada; Citibank; Brazil's Opportunity bank and pension funds owned by Banco do Brasil - offered 338.5 million reais for the largely rural area.
But still to come are the choice concessions in Sao Paulo city and state, Rio de Janeiro and Espirito Santo states and Minas Gerais state, hotly contested areas where experts predict large premiums.
The opening of Brazil's cellular sector has drawn the interest of major global operators and the government in April received bids from 15 foreign and local groups on the 10 B Band concessions.
The area 7 contract "is just the first part of a big game in wireless in Brazil," said Humberto Baranek of local bank Banco Pactual.

On Wednesday, five of the 15 groups were disqualified for failing to provide sufficient financial guarantees, prove members had legally formed a consortium or use an official Brazilian translator for a document.
They have five days to appeal the decision but analysts said the disqualified groups will now be hard-put to fight their way back into the B Band selloff.
"I don't think you can count them out completely but it put them in a difficult position. They have an uphill battle to get back in," Baranek said. "This is a major blow."

Valentino said the government had hoped 80 percent of those bidding would qualify but in the end fewer than 70 percent did. Three of the five consortia deemed unsuited to bid had made offers on the largest areas.

The process trimmed Tess, Algar and MCOM groups, which had planned to compete for Sao Paulo and Rio concessions, but would not hurt the selloff process or jeopardize potentially huge premiums, Valentino said.
"There's more than enough bidders. Besides, the envelopes are already in," he added.
Nonetheless, analysts expect tough legal battles ahead and possibly slow progress in awarding contracts on the major concession areas.
